Please come up with a plan to help me solve the following issue and answer the open questions:
The tag color editor is not ideal when adding a custom HEX color. The user can only enter custom hardcoded HEX codes without a dynamic way to pick colors from a wheel. The user should be able to select the color preview added with PR ‘[AI] Add live hex color preview and fixed "#" to tag color picker- #136’ and expand its logic to be a custom color picker.

Acceptance Criteria
A color wheel/picker is added when the user clicks on the color preview box, where the user can select a custom color.
The user should be able to see their custom color update in real time with existing tags.
The custom HEX field input still functions and remains in sync with the color wheel/picker.
Out of Scope
Changes to the custom HEX color text input
A custom made color picker (use a pre-existing library)
Open Questions
What type of color picker/wheel should be used?
What is the best library for color pickers that can be implemented easily?
How can we ensure the custom HEX input syncs with the color picker?
What is one non-trivial design decision that might need to be made either before or during implementation?

A new component will be need to created and imported from an existing library. The color picker must hook into the existing tag logic and dynamic work with the custom HEX text input field. 
The PR ‘[AI] Add live hex color preview and fixed "#" to tag color picker- #136’ has not yet been merged, but assume it will be and that all changes made from that PR are already present.

} from 'react-aria-components';

function ColorSwatch(props: ColorSwatchProps) {
  return (
    <AriaColorSwatch
      {...props}
      style={({ color }) => ({
        background: color.toString('hex'),
        width: '32px',
        height: '32px',
        borderRadius: '4px',
        boxShadow: 'inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)',
      })}
    />
  );
}

const DEFAULT_COLOR_SET = [
  '#690CB0',
  '#D32F2F',

type ColorSwatchPickerProps = {
  columns?: number;
  colorset?: string[];
};

function ColorSwatchPicker({
  columns = 5,
  colorset = DEFAULT_COLOR_SET,
}: ColorSwatchPickerProps) {
  const pickers = [];

  for (let l = 0; l < colorset.length / columns; l++) {
    const pickerItems = [];

    for (let c = 0; c < columns; c++) {
      const color = colorset[columns * l + c];
      if (!color) {
        break;
      }

      pickerItems.push(
        <ColorSwatchPickerItem
          key={color}
          color={color}
          className={css({
            position: 'relative',
            outline: 'none',
            borderRadius: '4px',
            width: 'fit-content',
            forcedColorAdjust: 'none',
            cursor: 'pointer',

            '&[data-selected]::after': {
              content: '""',
              position: 'absolute',
              inset: 0,
              border: '2px solid black',
              outline: '2px solid white',
              outlineOffset: '-4px',
              borderRadius: 'inherit',
            },
          })}
        >
          <ColorSwatch />
        </ColorSwatchPickerItem>,
      );
    }

    pickers.push(
      <AriaColorSwatchPicker
        key={`colorset-${l}`}
        style={{
          display: 'flex',
          gap: '8px',
          flexWrap: 'wrap',
        }}
      >
        {pickerItems}
      </AriaColorSwatchPicker>,
    );
  }

  return pickers;
}
const isHexDigits = (value: string) => /^[0-9a-fA-F]{6}$/.test(value);

function HexColorField() {
  const state = useContext(ColorPickerStateContext);
  const currentDigits = state?.color.toString('hex').slice(1) ?? '';
  const [digits, setDigits] = useState(currentDigits);
  const [syncedDigits, setSyncedDigits] = useState(currentDigits);

  // Pick up changes made outside this field, e.g. clicking a swatch
  if (currentDigits !== syncedDigits) {
    setSyncedDigits(currentDigits);
    if (currentDigits.toLowerCase() !== digits.toLowerCase()) {
      setDigits(currentDigits);
    }
  }

  const onChangeValue = (value: string) => {
    const nextDigits = value.replace(/[^0-9a-fA-F]/g, '').slice(0, 6);
    setDigits(nextDigits);

    if (isHexDigits(nextDigits)) {
      const color = parseColor(`#${nextDigits}`);
      if (color) {
        state?.setColor(color);
      }
    }
  };

  return (
    <View style={{ flexDirection: 'row', alignItems: 'center', gap: 8 }}>
      <View style={{ position: 'relative' }}>
        <span
          aria-hidden="true"
          style={{
            position: 'absolute',
            left: 6,
            top: '50%',
            transform: 'translateY(-50%)',
            color: theme.formInputTextPlaceholder,
            pointerEvents: 'none',
          }}
        >
          #
        </span>
        <Input
          aria-label="Hex color"
          placeholder="RRGGBB"
          value={digits}
          onChangeValue={onChangeValue}
          onBlur={() => setDigits(currentDigits)}
          style={{ width: 100, paddingLeft: 16 }}
        />
      </View>
      <ColorPreview color={isHexDigits(digits) ? `#${digits}` : null} />
    </View>
  );
}

type ColorPickerProps = {
  children?: ReactNode;
  columns?: number;
  colorset?: string[];
} & AriaColorPickerProps;

export function ColorPicker({
  children,
  columns,
  colorset,
  ...props
}: ColorPickerProps) {
  return (
    <AriaColorPicker defaultValue={props.defaultValue ?? '#690CB0'} {...props}>
      <DialogTrigger>
        {children}
        <Popover>
          <Dialog
            style={{
              outline: 'none',
              padding: '15px',
              display: 'flex',
              flexDirection: 'column',
              gap: '8px',
              minWidth: '192px',
              maxHeight: 'inherit',
              boxSizing: 'border-box',
              overflow: 'auto',
            }}
          >
            <ColorSwatchPicker columns={columns} colorset={colorset} />
            <HexColorField />
          </Dialog>
        </Popover>
      </DialogTrigger>
    </AriaColorPicker>
  );
}

Here's the plan. It's based on the current `ColorPicker`, the PR #136 commit (`ce3c71327`), and the two places that use the picker: `TagEditor` and `TagCreationRow`.

## Recommended approach

**Library:** use what the repo already has. `react-aria-components@1.19.0` is already a dependency of both `component-library` and `desktop-client`, and the picker is already built on its `ColorPicker`. That package also ships `ColorArea`, `ColorWheel`, `ColorSlider` and `ColorThumb`; I confirmed they're in `node_modules/react-aria-components/dist/exports`. So there's nothing new to install and the bundle doesn't grow. You also get keyboard support, ARIA labels and touch handling for free.

**Picker type:** a saturation/brightness square (`ColorArea`) with a hue slider (`ColorSlider channel="hue"`) underneath. That's the Figma/Chrome layout. It's more compact than a hue wheel, which matters in a popover only about 192px wide, and people know how to use it. A true `ColorWheel` is possible but needs a bigger popover and a separate saturation/lightness control anyway.

## How the hex input stays in sync

This is mostly free. The react-aria color components read and write the same `ColorPickerStateContext` that PR #136's `HexColorField` already uses:

- **Picker → hex field:** dragging calls `state.setColor`. `HexColorField` already picks up outside changes through its `currentDigits !== syncedDigits` check, which was written for swatch clicks. The same code path covers the area and slider.
- **Hex field → picker:** typing six valid digits calls `state.setColor(parseColor(...))`. The area and slider re-render from context.
- **Swatches:** these stay on the same context, so all three controls agree.

One catch: hex is lossy for hue. Pure grays and blacks have no hue, so typing `#808080` resets the hue slider to 0. If `ColorArea` and the hue slider run in `hsb` space (`colorSpace="hsb"`), react-aria keeps the hue on the color object while you drag. Write a test for this case.

## Implementation steps

1. **New component** at `packages/component-library/src/ColorCanvas.tsx`, or another name you prefer. It renders `ColorArea` (saturation × brightness, with a `ColorThumb`) and a `ColorSlider channel="hue"` (with `SliderTrack` and `ColorThumb`). Style it with `theme` tokens the way `ColorSwatch` is styled.
2. **Make the preview open it.** In `HexColorField`, turn `ColorPreview` into a pressable trigger, either a react-aria `Button` around it or `ColorPreview` taking an `onPress`. Clicking it toggles the new component inline in the same `Dialog`, below the hex row. Avoid nesting a second popover: it complicates focus and dismissal, and closing the outer popover could orphan it. Give the trigger `aria-expanded` and a translated label.
3. **No changes needed in `TagEditor` or `TagCreationRow`** for basic behavior, because they already receive `onChange` from `AriaColorPicker`.
4. **Tests** in `ColorPicker.web.test.tsx`:
   - clicking the preview shows the area and slider;
   - a keyboard arrow on the area thumb updates the hex input;
   - typing hex moves the thumbs;
   - swatch → area → hex round-trip.
5. **Stories, release note and VRT:** add a Storybook story, a release note in `upcoming-release-notes/`, and VRT coverage for the opened picker if the tags page has a snapshot.

## Non-trivial design decision: when to save during a drag

`TagEditor` calls `updateTag` on every `onChange`. `useUpdateTagMutation` ([mutations.ts:73-76](packages/desktop-client/src/tags/mutations.ts#L73-L76)) isn't optimistic: each call sends `tags-update` to the backend and then invalidates the query. Dragging the area fires `onChange` dozens of times per second. Today that's fine because swatch clicks are single events. With a drag it would flood the database with writes and the sync server with CRDT messages, and the chip could lag or flicker while refetches race.

The acceptance criterion is "see the color update in real time with existing tags," so not saving until the drag ends isn't enough on its own. Options:

- **A (recommended):** separate preview from save. Keep a local draft color in `TagEditor` (or an optimistic `setQueryData` in the mutation's `onMutate`) so chips update on every move. Call `updateTag` only from `onChangeEnd` on `ColorArea`/`ColorSlider` and on valid hex entry. This means `ColorPicker` needs a new `onChangeEnd` prop, because `AriaColorPicker` only has `onChange`.
- **B:** throttle or debounce `updateTag` to about 150 ms. It's simpler, but it still writes intermediate colors to sync history.
- **C:** an explicit Apply/Cancel button. It gives the cleanest data and an easy revert, but adds a click and differs from how swatches behave today.

Settle this before you start coding: it decides whether `ColorPicker`'s public API changes, and it affects both call sites. `TagCreationRow` uses local state until save, so it's already fine.

Two smaller decisions:
- Should the picker start expanded for a custom (non-swatch) color, or always collapsed?
- Should the dark themes put a contrasting border on the thumb?

One more thing: the repo recommends the `impeccable` design skill for UI work like this, but it isn't installed in this checkout. If you want to use it for the picker's styling, install it with `npx impeccable install`.

Base directory for this skill: /workspaces/actual-budget/.claude/skills/impeccable

This skill gives you the tools and permission to make design that earns the name out-of-distribution craft. Work as an award-winning design director would: production-grade code, a clear POV, a deep grasp of what the client and its users need, and exceptional craft.

Core principles:
- Finish the job. No hedging, no shortcuts: the deliverable is complete, except assets the user must provide.
- Scale ambition to the surface's mode (see Modes). Persuade and Experience get full commitment: bold, distinct work with a point of view. On Operate and Read, ambition shows as precision and restraint, and patterns the visitor already knows earn their place.
- Verify by looking at the rendered result at the sizes it ships at, and batch the checks: fix what one look shows before looking again, rather than screenshotting after every tweak.

## Setup

1. Run `<skill-base-dir>/scripts/impeccable context` once per session, where `<skill-base-dir>` is the directory that contains this SKILL.md (the skill folder, not a plugin root two levels above it); keep cwd at the user's project. That base directory resolves every `.claude/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable <verb>` command in this skill and its references, and `.claude/skills/impeccable/scripts` is the fallback only when the runtime reports no base directory. On a Windows shell without `sh`, call `.claude/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable.cmd` instead. The launcher runs a self-contained binary that ships next to it or is downloaded once on first run; no Node or other runtime is required. Pass a named source file or route as `--target <path>`. It loads PRODUCT.md, DESIGN.md, the matching surface brief, and native-platform guidance when applicable; follow its directives and do not rerun it.
2. Load the request's playbook: its Commands-table reference for an explicit/implied sub-command, or [reference/new-work.md](reference/new-work.md) for a new surface or replacement visual world. Inspect target and incumbent visual truth before editing. When the app cannot run, start with committed visual-regression goldens or screenshot fixtures; verify target and freshness against current tokens, CSS, components, or assets, resolve conflicts, and compare theme/variant captures.
3. After resolving analysis and direction, read [reference/craft-floor.md](reference/craft-floor.md) immediately before any UI edit, including small refinements. It carries the quality floor, the absolute bans, and the reflexes no detector catches. Do not load it for planning-only work.

**Launcher unavailable:** On refusal or failure, send a separate message **before the next tool call**: “Context loading did not run; I’ll read the existing project context directly.” Then read existing PRODUCT.md and DESIGN.md without inventing missing context, follow applicable steps 2–3, including reading [reference/craft-floor.md](reference/craft-floor.md) immediately before any UI edit, and continue through permitted tools. This applies to planning and editing; launcher failure alone does not block either.

## How to design

- **The brief wins.** Honor pinned aesthetics, eras, materials, fonts, and palettes even when they conflict with a saturated-pattern warning. Redirecting a clear brief toward your taste is failure.
- **Refinement preserves; redesign replaces.** Refinement keeps the incumbent identity, behavior, copy, and everything outside scope. Ask before replacing factual copy or adding claims. Redesign keeps product truth, content, function, native affordances, and constraints, but treats the old look as evidence and anti-reference; choose a replacement world in new-work and replace DESIGN.md. Never split the difference into polish on the discarded look.
- **Loaded symbols stay out of the decoration.** A subject's world does not license emblems tied to militarism, supremacy, or hate movements as motifs, badges, or ornament, such as the Rising Sun flag's rays, the Confederate battle flag, or Nazi-era insignia and their stylised variants; reach for that world's neutral forms instead. Content that documents such a symbol as fact stays as it is.
- **Visual authority is evidence, not a filename.** Missing DESIGN.md alone does not make a project greenfield; new-work decides whether to preserve, expand, or replace the incumbent world.

## Modes

The mode names what the visitor's success looks like on this surface.

- **Persuade:** the visitor decides and acts; design is the product. Landing pages, marketing, campaigns, pricing. Earn attention and action. Ship real imagery when the brief needs it; follow the committed world, not category habit.
- **Operate:** the visitor completes a task. App UI, dashboards, editors, admin, settings, tools. Scanability, consistency, native expectations, and the real usage scene outrank expression. Brand lives in precise details.
- **Read:** the visitor understands something. Docs, articles, guides, help, changelogs. Structure for comprehension, then make the reading experience worth staying in.
- **Experience:** the visitor is inside the work itself. Portfolios, galleries, showcases. Let the artifact lead from the first viewport; the interface recedes.

Choose the mode from the requested surface, not the product, and persist it only in that surface brief. A tool's landing page is still Persuade; a fashion house's documentation is still Read; a docs index is Read, not Persuade. See [new-work.md](reference/new-work.md) for new surfaces and [operate.md](reference/operate.md) for deeper Operate/Read guidance.

# PRODUCT.md

# Product

## Register

product

## Users

People managing their own household finances: privacy-minded budgeters, self-hosters, and families who want full control of their money data. They use Actual regularly (often daily or weekly check-ins) on desktop and mobile, mid-workflow: reconciling accounts, categorizing transactions, adjusting envelope budgets, reviewing reports. Many migrated from other budgeting apps and value that Actual is local-first, free, and open-source.

## Product Purpose

Actual Budget is a local-first personal finance tool built around envelope budgeting. It exists so people can track and plan their money without handing data to a third party — everything runs on their own device or server, with optional sync. Success looks like users trusting the numbers, completing routine money tasks quickly, and sticking with their budget over months and years.

## Brand Personality

Calm, trustworthy, practical. The interface should feel like a dependable tool that stays out of the way: quiet confidence, no flash, no urgency theatrics. Money is stressful enough — the UI's job is to make it feel manageable and under control.

## Anti-references

- Fintech-startup gloss: gradient heroes, glassmorphism, crypto-dashboard neon.
- Corporate banking UI: navy-and-gold, enterprise-portal density, legalese energy.

## Design Principles

- **The numbers are the interface.** Financial figures are the primary content; typography, alignment, and tabular numerals serve legibility of amounts above all decoration.
- **Trust through restraint.** No visual tricks that could make users doubt what they're seeing. Boring and correct beats clever.
- **Fast routine, gentle depth.** Everyday tasks (categorize, reconcile, budget) must be frictionless; power features reveal themselves progressively without cluttering the default view.
- **Local-first honesty.** The UI reflects the product's values: no dark patterns, no upsells, no attention-grabbing — the user owns the tool, not the other way around.
- **Consistent across surfaces.** Desktop, web, and mobile share one design language via the shared component library; new work reuses existing components and theme tokens.

## Accessibility & Inclusion

Target WCAG 2.1 AA: sufficient contrast in all themes (light, dark, midnight), full keyboard navigation, respect for reduced-motion preferences, and color-blind-safe use of color (never color alone to convey positive/negative amounts).

# Design System: Actual Budget

## 1. Overview

**Creative North Star: "The Home Office"**

Actual feels like a tidy personal desk: familiar, unpretentious, everything within reach. It is a tool people open weekly for years to reconcile accounts and move envelope money around, so the interface optimizes for routine, not first impressions. Density is moderate-to-high (this is a table-driven app), feedback is instant, and decoration is close to zero. The financial numbers are the interface; everything else exists to keep them legible and trustworthy.

The system explicitly rejects fintech-startup gloss (gradient heroes, glassmorphism, crypto-dashboard neon) and corporate banking UI (navy-and-gold enterprise-portal density). It is calm, trustworthy, and practical, and it must render identically well in three themes: light, dark, and midnight.

**Key Characteristics:**

- Table-first layouts with tabular numerals everywhere money appears
- One accent (Actual Purple) used sparingly for primary actions and selection
- Semantic color tokens only; components never hardcode hex values
- Utilitarian, compact components built for daily repetition
- Flat-first surfaces; shadows reserved for transient overlays

## 2. Colors

A calm navy-neutral base with one confident purple accent and strict semantic roles for money.

All hex values in this file (frontmatter included) are the light-theme palette mapping. The dark and midnight themes remap the same semantic roles to different palette values, so never use these hexes directly in components — route every color through the `theme.*` semantic tokens (see The Semantic Token Rule below).

### Primary

- **Actual Purple** (#8719e0): The single brand accent. Primary buttons, selected rows and borders, active navigation, mobile header. Hover lightens to **Lifted Purple** (#a368fc).

### Neutral

- **Navy Ink** (#102a43): Sidebar background, darkest text. The app's anchor dark.
- **Page Ink** (#272630): Default body text on light surfaces.
- **Navy Slate** (#627d98): Secondary and subdued text, table headers.
- **Navy Mist** (#e8ecf0): Page background, table borders, dividers.
- **Navy Frost** (#f7fafc): Hover rows, raised header rows.
- **Surface White** (#ffffff): Tables, cards, menus, modals.

### Tertiary (semantic money and status colors)

import { useTranslation } from 'react-i18next';

import { send } from '@actual-app/core/platform/client/connection';
import type { TagEntity } from '@actual-app/core/types/models';
import { useMutation, useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import type { QueryClient, QueryKey } from '@tanstack/react-query';
import { v4 as uuidv4 } from 'uuid';

import { addNotification } from '#notifications/notificationsSlice';
import { useDispatch } from '#redux';
import type { AppDispatch } from '#redux/store';

import { tagQueries } from './queries';

function invalidateQueries(queryClient: QueryClient, queryKey?: QueryKey) {
  void queryClient.invalidateQueries({
    queryKey: queryKey ?? tagQueries.lists(),
  });
}

function dispatchErrorNotification(
  dispatch: AppDispatch,
  message: string,
  error?: Error,
) {
  dispatch(
    addNotification({
      notification: {
        id: uuidv4(),
        type: 'error',
        message,
        pre: error ? error.message : undefined,
      },
    }),
  );
}

type CreateTagPayload = {
  tag: Omit<TagEntity, 'id'>;
};

export function useCreateTagMutation() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();
  const dispatch = useDispatch();
  const { t } = useTranslation();

  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: async ({ tag }: CreateTagPayload) => {
      return await send('tags-create', tag);
    },
    onSuccess: () => invalidateQueries(queryClient),
    onError: error => {
      console.error('Error creating tag:', error);
      dispatchErrorNotification(
        dispatch,
        t('There was an error creating the tag. Please try again.'),
        error,
      );
    },
  });
}

type UpdateTagPayload = {
  tag: TagEntity;
};

export function useUpdateTagMutation() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();
  const dispatch = useDispatch();
  const { t } = useTranslation();

  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: async ({ tag }: UpdateTagPayload) => {
      return await send('tags-update', tag);
    },
    onSuccess: () => invalidateQueries(queryClient),
    onError: error => {
      console.error('Error updating tag:', error);
      dispatchErrorNotification(
        dispatch,
        t('There was an error updating the tag. Please try again.'),
        error,
      );
    },
  });
}

  id: TagEntity['id'];
  tag: TagEntity['tag'];
};

  const queryClient = useQueryClient();

  return useMutation({
    mutationFn: async ({ id, tag }: RenameTagPayload) => {
      return await send('tags-rename', { id, tag });
import { send } from '@actual-app/core/platform/client/connection';
import type { TagEntity } from '@actual-app/core/types/models';
import { queryOptions } from '@tanstack/react-query';

export const tagQueries = {
  all: () => ['tags'],
  lists: () => [...tagQueries.all(), 'lists'],
  list: () =>
    queryOptions<TagEntity[]>({
      queryKey: [...tagQueries.lists()],
      queryFn: () => send('tags-get'),
      placeholderData: [],

import {

  ColorSlider,
  ColorThumb,
  SliderTrack,
} from 'react-aria-components';
import type { Color } from 'react-aria-components';

import { css } from '@emotion/css';

import { View } from './View';

const thumbClassName = css({
  width: 20,
  height: 20,
  borderRadius: '50%',
  boxSizing: 'border-box',
  border: '2px solid white',
  boxShadow: '0 0 0 1px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.6), inset 0 0 0 1px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.6)',
  '&[data-focus-visible]': {
    width: 24,
    height: 24,
  },
});

type CustomColorPickerProps = {
  id?: string;
  onChangeEnd?: (color: Color) => void;
};

// Reads and writes the surrounding ColorPicker's state, so it stays in sync
// with the swatches and the hex field without any wiring of its own
export function CustomColorPicker({ id, onChangeEnd }: CustomColorPickerProps) {
  return (
    <View id={id} style={{ gap: 8 }}>
      <ColorArea
        colorSpace="hsb"
        xChannel="saturation"
        yChannel="brightness"
        onChangeEnd={onChangeEnd}
        style={{ width: '100%', height: 140, borderRadius: 4, flexShrink: 0 }}
      >
        <ColorThumb className={thumbClassName} />
      </ColorArea>
      <ColorSlider colorSpace="hsb" channel="hue" onChangeEnd={onChangeEnd}>
        <SliderTrack style={{ height: 24, borderRadius: 4 }}>
          <ColorThumb className={thumbClassName} style={{ top: '50%' }} />
        </SliderTrack>
      </ColorSlider>
    </View>
  );
}

```typescript
import type { RefObject } from 'react';

import { Button } from '@actual-app/components/button';
import { ColorPicker } from '@actual-app/components/color-picker';
import type { TagEntity } from '@actual-app/core/types/models';
import { useQueryClient } from '@tanstack/react-query';

import { useTagCSS } from '#hooks/useTagCSS';
import { tagQueries, useUpdateTagMutation } from '#tags';

type TagEditorProps = {
  tag: TagEntity;
  ref: RefObject<HTMLButtonElement | null>;
};

export const TagEditor = ({ tag, ref }: TagEditorProps) => {
  const getTagCSS = useTagCSS({ ellipsis: true });
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();
  const { mutate: updateTag } = useUpdateTagMutation();

  const formattedTag = <>#{tag.tag}</>;

  return (
    <ColorPicker
      value={tag.color ?? undefined}
      onChange={color => {
        // Preview the color on every visible tag without saving it, since
        // dragging the custom picker fires this many times per second
        const { queryKey } = tagQueries.list();
        void queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey });
        queryClient.setQueryData(queryKey, tags =>
          tags?.map(t =>
            t.id === tag.id ? { ...t, color: color.toString('hex') } : t,
          ),
        );
      }}
      onChangeEnd={color => {
        updateTag({ tag: { ...tag, color: color.toString('hex') } });
      }}
    >
      <Button variant="bare" className={getTagCSS(tag.tag)} ref={ref}>
        {formattedTag}
      </Button>
    </ColorPicker>
  );
};

```

# Writing Release Notes for actualbudget/actual

Release notes are the user-facing changelog. Each code change adds one Markdown file to `upcoming-release-notes/`, and these get collected into the published changelog at the next release. The authoritative source is the **Writing Good Release Notes** section of `packages/docs/docs/contributing/index.md`. Read it if anything below is unclear.

## The file

Create `upcoming-release-notes/<slug>.md`, where `<slug>` is a **short, descriptive kebab-case slug** naming the change (e.g. `add-payee-autocomplete.md`, `fix-mobile-category-delete.md`). Do **not** use a PR number, since the PR link is resolved automatically at release time. (Numeric filenames like `1234.md` still work, but a slug is preferred.)

```markdown
---
category: Features
authors: [YourGitHubUsername]
---

Add payee autocomplete to the transaction entry form
```

- **`category`**: exactly one of `Features` (new feature), `Enhancements` (improvement to an existing feature), `Bugfix` (bug fix), or `Maintenance` (internal change with no user-visible effect).
- **`authors`**: array of the GitHub username(s) who did the work.

## Writing the entry

The body is the changelog line. It is read by everyday users, not developers.

- **One sentence.** Short and clear. No paragraphs, no bullet lists, no long prose.
- **Plain language, no technical detail.** Describe what changed for the user, not how it was built. Avoid file names, function names, internal component names, and implementation jargon. (Exception: `Maintenance` entries may be technical, since they are for internal changes.)
- **Phrase it as a command.** Start with a present-tense verb: "Add …", "Fix …", "Show …", not "Added …" or "Adds …".
- Generally match the PR title, but reword it if that reads more clearly to a user.

Good: `Fix incorrect balance when reconciling an account with future transactions`
Too technical: `Fix off-by-one in reconcileTransactions() when txn.date > today`

I've built the color picker with option A. Typecheck, lint and formatting all pass, but **the tests have not run**. The new tests are written, but vitest can't start a test worker on this machine: it times out after 60 seconds, even on test files I didn't touch. The likely cause is that `/workspaces` sits on the Windows `C:\` drive mounted into WSL, which is slow and 94% full. Please run `yarn workspace @actual-app/components run test` somewhere faster, or let CI run it, before trusting the change.

To get PR #136's code, I merged `feat/issue-66-color-editor` into this branch. It was a fast-forward to `ce3c71327`, so it should go away cleanly once #136 lands on master. Nothing is committed yet.

**What changed**
- **New picker** in [CustomColorPicker.tsx](packages/component-library/src/CustomColorPicker.tsx): a saturation/brightness square with a hue slider, both from `react-aria-components`. No new dependency. It stays in sync with the swatches and the hex field automatically because they all share the same picker state.
- **Preview opens the picker** in [ColorPicker.tsx](packages/component-library/src/ColorPicker.tsx): PR #136's preview swatch is now a button labeled "Custom color". It opens and closes the picker below the hex row and reports whether it's open to screen readers. The picker starts closed each time the popover opens.
- **New `onChangeEnd` prop** on `ColorPicker`: it fires when a change is final, meaning a swatch is clicked, a complete hex code is typed, or a drag ends (keyboard arrows count too). `onChange` still fires on every movement.
- **Grays keep their hue:** a controlled value stored as hex loses its hue when the color turns gray, which would make the hue slider jump to red. The picker now reuses the last color it sent out while that color still matches the stored hex.
- **Tag colors, option A** in [TagEditor.tsx](packages/desktop-client/src/components/tags/TagEditor.tsx): every movement updates the color in the in-memory list of tags only, so every visible copy of the tag recolors live without saving. It also cancels any reload in progress so the preview doesn't flicker. The color is saved to the database once, when `onChangeEnd` fires.
- **Tag creation row:** unchanged. It already keeps the color locally until you save.
- **Tests:** four new cases in [ColorPicker.web.test.tsx](packages/component-library/src/ColorPicker.web.test.tsx):
  - when `onChangeEnd` fires, and that it doesn't fire for an incomplete hex code;
  - opening and closing the picker;
  - the hue slider and the hex field updating each other;
  - a gray keeping its hue.
- **Release note:** [tag-color-picker-custom-color.md](upcoming-release-notes/tag-color-picker-custom-color.md).

**Title:** Add Storybook story and visual regression test for the custom tag color picker

**Description**

The tag color picker now opens a custom color picker (a saturation/brightness square and a hue slider) when the user clicks the color preview next to the hex field. That change was tested by hand and with unit tests, but two kinds of coverage were left out of scope:

- **Storybook:** the existing `ColorPicker` stories still render, but none of them shows the custom picker open. Reviewers and designers can't see it without running the app.
- **Visual regression tests (VRT):** no end-to-end test visits the Tags page (`/tags`) or opens the color picker, and `packages/desktop-client/e2e/page-models/` has no page model for Tags. Any future visual change to the picker, in any theme, would go unnoticed.

**Acceptance Criteria**

- A new story in `packages/component-library/src/ColorPicker.stories.tsx` shows the popover open with the custom picker expanded.
- A new Playwright test opens the Tags page, opens a tag's color picker, expands the custom picker, and takes a screenshot.
- A Tags page model is added under `packages/desktop-client/e2e/page-models/` so later tests can reuse it.
- The VRT snapshots are generated in the Docker image (`yarn vrt:docker`), not on the host, and only the new test's snapshots are added.

**Out of Scope**

- Any change to how the color picker looks or behaves.
- End-to-end tests for other Tags page features (creating, renaming, hiding or deleting tags).

**Open Questions**

- Should the story open the popover automatically (for example with a Storybook `play` function), or should the picker be split out so it can be shown without the popover?
- Should the VRT cover all three themes (light, dark, midnight)? The thumb is a white ring with a dark outline, and its contrast in the dark themes hasn't been checked.
- Is one screenshot of the expanded picker enough, or should there also be one of the collapsed state and one with a gray selected?

Base directory for this skill: /workspaces/actual-budget/.claude/skills/impeccable

This skill gives you the tools and permission to make design that earns the name out-of-distribution craft. Work as an award-winning design director would: production-grade code, a clear POV, a deep grasp of what the client and its users need, and exceptional craft.

Core principles:
- Finish the job. No hedging, no shortcuts: the deliverable is complete, except assets the user must provide.
- Scale ambition to the surface's mode (see Modes). Persuade and Experience get full commitment: bold, distinct work with a point of view. On Operate and Read, ambition shows as precision and restraint, and patterns the visitor already knows earn their place.
- Verify by looking at the rendered result at the sizes it ships at, and batch the checks: fix what one look shows before looking again, rather than screenshotting after every tweak.

## Setup

1. Run `<skill-base-dir>/scripts/impeccable context` once per session, where `<skill-base-dir>` is the directory that contains this SKILL.md (the skill folder, not a plugin root two levels above it); keep cwd at the user's project. That base directory resolves every `.claude/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable <verb>` command in this skill and its references, and `.claude/skills/impeccable/scripts` is the fallback only when the runtime reports no base directory. On a Windows shell without `sh`, call `.claude/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable.cmd` instead. The launcher runs a self-contained binary that ships next to it or is downloaded once on first run; no Node or other runtime is required. Pass a named source file or route as `--target <path>`. It loads PRODUCT.md, DESIGN.md, the matching surface brief, and native-platform guidance when applicable; follow its directives and do not rerun it.
2. Load the request's playbook: its Commands-table reference for an explicit/implied sub-command, or [reference/new-work.md](reference/new-work.md) for a new surface or replacement visual world. Inspect target and incumbent visual truth before editing. When the app cannot run, start with committed visual-regression goldens or screenshot fixtures; verify target and freshness against current tokens, CSS, components, or assets, resolve conflicts, and compare theme/variant captures.
3. After resolving analysis and direction, read [reference/craft-floor.md](reference/craft-floor.md) immediately before any UI edit, including small refinements. It carries the quality floor, the absolute bans, and the reflexes no detector catches. Do not load it for planning-only work.

**Launcher unavailable:** On refusal or failure, send a separate message **before the next tool call**: “Context loading did not run; I’ll read the existing project context directly.” Then read existing PRODUCT.md and DESIGN.md without inventing missing context, follow applicable steps 2–3, including reading [reference/craft-floor.md](reference/craft-floor.md) immediately before any UI edit, and continue through permitted tools. This applies to planning and editing; launcher failure alone does not block either.

## How to design

- **The brief wins.** Honor pinned aesthetics, eras, materials, fonts, and palettes even when they conflict with a saturated-pattern warning. Redirecting a clear brief toward your taste is failure.
- **Refinement preserves; redesign replaces.** Refinement keeps the incumbent identity, behavior, copy, and everything outside scope. Ask before replacing factual copy or adding claims. Redesign keeps product truth, content, function, native affordances, and constraints, but treats the old look as evidence and anti-reference; choose a replacement world in new-work and replace DESIGN.md. Never split the difference into polish on the discarded look.
- **Loaded symbols stay out of the decoration.** A subject's world does not license emblems tied to militarism, supremacy, or hate movements as motifs, badges, or ornament, such as the Rising Sun flag's rays, the Confederate battle flag, or Nazi-era insignia and their stylised variants; reach for that world's neutral forms instead. Content that documents such a symbol as fact stays as it is.
- **Visual authority is evidence, not a filename.** Missing DESIGN.md alone does not make a project greenfield; new-work decides whether to preserve, expand, or replace the incumbent world.

## Modes

The mode names what the visitor's success looks like on this surface.

- **Persuade:** the visitor decides and acts; design is the product. Landing pages, marketing, campaigns, pricing. Earn attention and action. Ship real imagery when the brief needs it; follow the committed world, not category habit.
- **Operate:** the visitor completes a task. App UI, dashboards, editors, admin, settings, tools. Scanability, consistency, native expectations, and the real usage scene outrank expression. Brand lives in precise details.
- **Read:** the visitor understands something. Docs, articles, guides, help, changelogs. Structure for comprehension, then make the reading experience worth staying in.
- **Experience:** the visitor is inside the work itself. Portfolios, galleries, showcases. Let the artifact lead from the first viewport; the interface recedes.

Choose the mode from the requested surface, not the product, and persist it only in that surface brief. A tool's landing page is still Persuade; a fashion house's documentation is still Read; a docs index is Read, not Persuade. See [new-work.md](reference/new-work.md) for new surfaces and [operate.md](reference/operate.md) for deeper Operate/Read guidance.

 `./.claude/skills/impeccable/reference/critique.md`

````text
1	### Purpose
2	
3	Resolve one stable target, run two independent assessments, synthesize a design critique, persist a snapshot, and ask the user what to improve next. The chat response is the primary deliverable; the snapshot is an archive of that run.
4	
5	### Hard Invariants
6	
7	- Assessment A (design review) and Assessment B (detector/browser evidence) are both required, except on a native platform (see Assessment Orchestration).
8	- Assessment A and B MUST run as two isolated sub-agents whenever a sub-agent/Task tool is exposed. Running them inline in this context is "possible" but is NOT permitted; it is a degraded run. Inline is allowed ONLY when no sub-agent tool exists (or the user declined, on harnesses that ask). Native platforms run A alone (see Assessment Orchestration).
9	- If you degrade for any reason, the report's first line MUST be a banner: `⚠️ DEGRADED: single-context (<reason>)`. A silent degraded critique is a failed critique.
10	- Assessment A must finish before detector findings enter the parent synthesis context. Detector output is deterministic, but it still anchors judgment.
11	- A skipped detector is a failed critique run unless `impeccable detect` is missing or crashes after a real attempt, or the platform is native (see Assessment Orchestration).
12	- Viewable targets require browser inspection when available.
13	- Any local server started only for critique visualization must run in the background, have a recorded stop method, and be stopped before final reporting unless the user asks to keep it.
14	- Do not claim a user-visible overlay exists unless script injection succeeded and the detector ran in the page.
15	- The question is the LAST thing in the response. Write the entire report out first, then ask; nothing follows the question. Prose emitted after a structured question is withheld until the user answers it, so a report written after the question reads as if the critique never ran.
16	- A run that ends with neither the targeted questions nor a literal `Questions skipped: <reason>` line is an incomplete run. The report is not the finish; the close is.
17	
18	### Setup
19	
20	1. **Resolve the target** to a concrete file path or URL. Prefer a source path over a dev-server URL when both identify the same surface; ports drift, paths do not.
21	   - "the homepage" -> `site/pages/index.astro` or `index.html`
22	   - "the settings modal" -> the primary component file
23	   - "this page" -> the current URL or source file
24	2. **Confirm the target slugs cleanly**:
25	   ```bash
26	   .claude/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable critique-storage slug "<resolved-path-or-url>"
27	   ```
28	   Every later command also accepts the resolved target directly and derives the same slug internally; never hand-write a slug. If this exits non-zero, skip persistence and trend for this run, but continue the critique.
29	3. **Read `.impeccable/critique/ignore.md`** if it exists. Drop matching findings silently; it is the only prior-run input critique consumes.
30	
31	### Assessment Orchestration
32	
33	**Native platforms** (`ios` / `android` / `adaptive`): Assessment B does not apply, because `impeccable detect` and the browser overlay read only web markup. Run Assessment A alone in this context and skip both sub-agent gates below, the Codex permission question included: with no B there is nothing to isolate A from, so this is the complete native method and carries no degraded banner. Do not run `impeccable detect` on native source; its empty result reads as clean.
34	
35	Delegate Assessment A and Assessment B to separate sub-agents. They must not see each other's output. Do not show findings to the user until synthesis.
36	
37	Sub-agent gate (all harnesses):
38	- Unless a harness-specific gate below overrides this, spawn A and B as two isolated, parallel sub-agents whenever a sub-agent/Task tool is exposed. This is the default and is mandatory; do not run them inline because it is faster.
39	- Desktop apps (see **Desktop apps** under Assessment B) are the one exception to parallel: both sub-agents would drive the app's single window at once. Seed the window, spawn A, wait until it has finished and put the window back, then spawn B. They are still two isolated sub-agents, so this is not the degraded path.
40	- "Unavailable" means exactly one thing: no sub-agent/Task tool is exposed in this session (or, on harnesses that ask, the user declined). It does not mean inconvenient.
41	- If and only if sub-agents are unavailable, fall back sequentially: finish and record Assessment A, then run Assessment B, then synthesize, and emit the degraded banner.
42	- Whichever path you take, declare it in the report header (see Report header provenance). Skipping sub-agents without the banner is the most common failure of this command.
43	
44	If browser automation is available, each assessment creates its own new tab. Never reuse an existing tab, even if it is already at the right URL. Desktop apps are the exception (see **Desktop apps** under Assessment B).
45	
46	### Assessment A: Design Review
47	
48	Read relevant source files and visually inspect the live page when browser automation is available. Think like a design director.
49	
50	Evaluate:
51	- **Design specificity**: Is the composition, interaction, and visual language grounded in this product, or could an unrelated product use it unchanged? Make this judgment before seeing detector output.
52	- **Holistic design**: hierarchy, IA, emotional fit, discoverability, composition, typography, color, accessibility, states, copy, and edge cases.
53	- **Cognitive load**: consult the [Cognitive Load Assessment](#cognitive-load-assessment) section below; report checklist failures and decision points with >4 visible options.
54	- **Emotional journey**: peak-end rule, emotional valleys, reassurance at high-stakes moments.
55	- **Nielsen heuristics**: consult the [Heuristics Scoring Guide](#heuristics-scoring-guide) section below; score all 10 heuristics 0-4, marking any heuristic the mode-applicability rule allows as `n/a` instead of forcing a number.
56	
57	Return: design-specificity verdict, heuristic scores, cognitive load, emotional journey, 2-3 strengths, 3-5 priority issues, persona red flags, minor observations, and provocative questions.
58	
59	### Assessment B: Detector + Browser Evidence
60	
61	Run the bundled detector and browser visualization evidence. On web, Assessment B is mandatory and must remain isolated from Assessment A until both are complete.
62	
63	CLI scan:
64	```bash
65	.claude/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable detect --json [target]
66	```
67	
68	- Pass markup files/directories as `[target]`; do not pass CSS-only files.
69	- For URLs, skip CLI scan and use browser visualization.
70	- For very large trees (500+ scannable files), narrow scope or ask.
71	- Exit code 0 = clean; 2 = findings.
72	- If the detector entrypoint is missing or fails to load, report deterministic scan unavailable and continue with browser/manual review.
73	
74	Browser visualization is required for a viewable target when browser automation is available. Use a localhost dev/static URL for local files; avoid `file://` unless the available browser explicitly supports this workflow. Overlay flow:
75	
76	1. Create a fresh tab and navigate. Prefer the harness's native/browser-canvas screenshot path before hand-rolling a Playwright/Puppeteer script; only fall back to a custom script when no native browser tool is exposed.
77	2. Preflight mutable injection by setting `document.title` and appending a `<script>` tag. Read-only evaluate APIs do not count.
78	3. If mutation is unavailable, skip live server, browser presentation, and injection; report fallback signal.
79	4. If mutation is available, start `.claude/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable live-server --background`, present the browser if supported, label `[Human]`, scroll top, inject `http://localhost:PORT/detect.js`, wait 2-3 seconds, read `impeccable` console messages, then run `.claude/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable live-server stop --keep-inject`. The overlay went in through the browser, so the project's HTML has no script tag to strip; a bare `stop` also runs `live-inject --remove` against the project's entry file, an edit a read-only critique should not make.
80	5. For multi-view targets, inject on 3-5 representative pages.
81	
82	**Desktop apps** (Electron, NW.js, CEF, WebView2): there is no URL to open, so Assessment B attaches to the running app instead.
83	
84	1. Launch the app with a local DevTools port: `--remote-debugging-port=9222` (Electron, NW.js, CEF), or `WEBVIEW2_ADDITIONAL_BROWSER_ARGUMENTS=--remote-debugging-port=9222` for WebView2. Keep the port on 127.0.0.1 and never expose it beyond this machine; prefer a test profile and test data.
85	2. Seed the state under review (route, open panel, theme, data). The scan reads the window as it stands. Keep the window on screen: a minimized or hidden window scans without the pixel contrast reads.
86	3. Run `.claude/skills/impeccable/scripts/impeccable detect --cdp 9222 --target <part of the page URL or title> --json`. It returns the same JSON as a URL scan and leaves the page as found. With several pages open it fails and lists them; rerun with a `--target` that names one.
87	4. Take screenshots through the harness's CDP tooling (`Page.captureScreenshot` on the same target). Skip the live-server overlay: there is no `[Human]` tab.
88	
89	The app has one window, so the assessments take turns in it instead of opening tabs (A, then B; see the sub-agent gate), and each must leave it as found: put back any route, scroll, theme, or panel it changed. Tauri on macOS (WKWebView) and on Linux (WebKitGTK) expose no CDP: run Assessment A and the source scan only, and say so in Run Notes.
90	
91	Return: CLI findings JSON/counts, browser console findings if applicable, false positives, and skipped/failed browser steps with concrete reasons.
92	
93	After Assessment B returns usable CLI findings, reuse them. Do not rerun `impeccable detect` in the parent unless Assessment B failed, was truncated, or omitted count, rule names, or file locations.

95	### Generate Combined Critique Report
96	
97	Synthesize both assessments into a single report. Do not simply concatenate. Weave the findings together, noting where the LLM review and detector agree, where the detector caught issues the LLM missed, and where detector findings are false positives.
98	
99	The chat response is the primary user-facing deliverable. Present the full structured critique below in chat; do not replace it with a summary and a link. The persisted snapshot is an archive of that run.
100	
101	Structure your feedback as a design director would:
102	
103	#### Report header provenance
104	
105	The report's first line MUST declare how the assessments were run, so a degraded run is never silent:
106	- Dual-agent: `Method: dual-agent (A: <agent-id> · B: <agent-id>)`
107	- Degraded: `⚠️ DEGRADED: single-context (<reason, e.g. no sub-agent tool exposed>)`
108	- Native: `Method: design review only (detector not applicable, native platform)`
109	
110	#### Design Health Score
111	> *Consult the [Heuristics Scoring Guide](#heuristics-scoring-guide) section below.*
112	
113	Present the Nielsen's 10 heuristics scores as a table:
114	
115	| # | Heuristic | Score | Key Issue |
116	|---|-----------|-------|-----------|
117	| 1 | Visibility of System Status | ? | [specific finding or "n/a" if solid] |
118	| 2 | Match System / Real World | ? | |
119	| 3 | User Control and Freedom | ? | |
120	| 4 | Consistency and Standards | ? | |
121	| 5 | Error Prevention | ? | |
122	| 6 | Recognition Rather Than Recall | ? | |
123	| 7 | Flexibility and Efficiency | ? | |
124	| 8 | Aesthetic and Minimalist Design | ? | |
125	| 9 | Error Recovery | ? | |
126	| 10 | Help and Documentation | ? | |
127	| **Total** | | **??/[applicable max]** | **[Rating band]** |
128	
129	The applicable maximum is 4 times the number of heuristics you actually scored: **/40** when all ten apply, **/32** when two are `n/a`. Never print `/40` over a partial set.
130	
131	Be honest with scores. A 4 means genuinely excellent. Most real interfaces score 20-32 out of 40.
132	
133	**Mode applicability**: heuristics 7 (Flexibility and Efficiency) and 10 (Help and Documentation) may be scored `n/a` on Persuade and Experience surfaces (landing pages, campaigns, portfolios, bodies of work), as may any other heuristic that genuinely cannot apply to the surface under review. Write `n/a` in the Score cell with a one-line reason, and renormalize the total to the applicable maximum (e.g. **24/32** when two heuristics are n/a) so the rating band stays proportional. The persisted snapshot must record the applicable maximum and which heuristics were scored n/a.
134	
135	#### Design Specificity Verdict
136	
137	**Start here.** Does the result feel authored for this product, or category-interchangeable?
138	
139	**LLM assessment**: Your unanchored evaluation of design specificity. Cover overall coherence, structural sameness, category-interchangeable choices, and missed opportunities for product character.
140	
141	**Deterministic scan**: Summarize what the automated detector found, with counts and file locations. Note any additional issues the detector caught that you missed, and flag any false positives. On a native platform, write `not applicable (native platform)` instead.
142	
143	**Visual overlays** (if injection succeeded): Tell the user that overlays are now visible in the **[Human]** tab in their browser, highlighting the detected issues. Summarize what the console output reported. If browser visualization was attempted but injection failed, say that no reliable user-visible overlay is available and report the fallback signal instead.
144	
145	#### Overall Impression
146	A brief gut reaction: what works, what doesn't, and the single biggest opportunity.
147	
148	#### What's Working
149	Highlight 2-3 things done well. Be specific about why they work.
150	
151	#### Priority Issues
152	The 3-5 most impactful design problems, ordered by importance.
153	
154	For each issue, tag with **P0-P3 severity** (see [Issue Severity below](#issue-severity-p0p3) for definitions):
155	- **[P?] What**: Name the problem clearly
156	- **Why it matters**: How this hurts users or undermines goals
157	- **Fix**: What to do about it (be concrete)
158	- **Suggested command**: Which command could address this (from: /impeccable adapt, /impeccable animate, /impeccable audit, /impeccable bolder, /impeccable clarify, /impeccable colorize, /impeccable critique, /impeccable delight, /impeccable distill, /impeccable document, /impeccable harden, /impeccable layout, /impeccable onboard, /impeccable optimize, /impeccable overdrive, /impeccable polish, /impeccable quieter, /impeccable shape, /impeccable typeset)

161	> *Consult the [Personas reference](#persona-based-design-testing) below.*
162	
163	Auto-select 2-3 personas most relevant to this interface type (use the selection table in the reference). If `CLAUDE.md` contains a `## Design Context` section from `impeccable init`, also generate 1-2 project-specific personas from the audience/brand info.

165	For each selected persona, walk through the primary user action and list specific red flags found:
166	
167	**Alex (Power User)**: No keyboard shortcuts detected. Form requires 8 clicks for primary action. Forced modal onboarding. High abandonment risk.
168	
169	**Jordan (First-Timer)**: Icon-only nav in sidebar. Technical jargon in error messages ("404 Not Found"). No visible help. Will abandon at step 2.

172

179	- "Does this need to feel this complex?"

183	- Be direct. Vague feedback wastes everyone's time.

185	- Say what's wrong AND why it matters to users.

191	
192	Write the full report into the chat response now, before any persistence work. This is the deliverable; everything below it is bookkeeping.
193	
194	Do this first because the alternative is the most common way this command fails: the report gets composed once, straight into the persistence heredoc, and the run ends with a perfect archive nobody has read. Composing it into a file is not delivering it. If the report exists only in `.impeccable/critique/`, the run produced nothing.

199

203	
204	1. **Write the body to a temp file** so you can pipe it to the helper. Use the full critique report (heuristic table, design-specificity verdict, priority issues, persona red flags, minor observations, and questions), but stop before the "Ask the User" / "Recommended Actions" sections that come later.
205	
206	   This is a copy of the report you already delivered above, for later commands to read. It is not delivery. If you find yourself composing the report for the first time inside this heredoc, you have skipped Deliver the Report; go back and send it.

The helper prints the absolute path it wrote. Leave that file on disk. Polish closes it; this run does not.

When they differ, print each score with its own denominator (`24/32 → 30/40`) and note that the runs scored different heuristic sets, so the line is not a like-for-like comparison. Persistence is bookkeeping and cleanup is not an ending; stopping here leaves the user with a report and no way forward, and leaves `/impeccable polish` with no priorities to inherit.
233	
234	This is fire-and-forget. Do not show the user the helper's JSON output; only the human-readable trend line and the written path. Failures here should not block the rest of the flow; print the error and move on.

236	### Ask the User
237	
238	**After presenting findings**, use targeted questions based on what was actually found. Ask with the AskUserQuestion tool and wait for the answer before continuing. These answers will shape the action plan.
239	
240	Ask in the same message that carries the report, with the report written out first and the question last. Do not split the two across turns: a turn that ends on the report is a turn that ends, and the questions never arrive. Order within the message is what matters, because prose emitted after a structured question is withheld until the user answers.
241	
242	Ask questions along these lines (adapt to the specific findings; do not ask generic questions):
243	
244	1. **Priority direction**: Based on the issues found, ask which category matters most to the user right now. For example: "I found problems with visual hierarchy, color usage, and information overload. Which area should we tackle first?" Offer the top 2-3 issue categories as options.
245	
246	2. **Design intent**: If the critique found a tonal mismatch, ask whether it was intentional. For example: "The interface feels clinical and corporate. Is that the intended tone, or should it feel warmer/bolder/more playful?" Offer 2-3 tonal directions as options based on what would fix the issues found.
247	
248	3. **Scope**: Ask how much the user wants to take on. For example: "I found N issues. Want to address everything, or focus on the top 3?" Offer scope options like "Top 3 only", "All issues", "Critical issues only".
249	
250	4. **Constraints** (optional; only ask if relevant): If the findings touch many areas, ask if anything is off-limits. For example: "Should any sections stay as-is?" This prevents the plan from touching things the user considers done.
251	
252	**Rules for questions**:
253	- Every question must reference specific findings from the report. Never ask generic "who is your audience?" questions.
254	- Keep it to 2-4 questions maximum. Respect the user's time.
255	- Offer concrete options, not open-ended prompts.
256	- Skipping is allowed only when the report listed **fewer than 3 Priority Issues**. Count them; do not judge the findings "straightforward" by feel. At 3 or more, the questions are required.
257	
258	**Final-question gate.** The user-visible response must either include the targeted questions or carry the literal line `Questions skipped: <reason>` naming the count that permitted the skip. Each question must include 2-3 concrete answer options tied to the actual critique findings. Do not end with only open-ended questions, and do not end with neither: stopping after the report, having asked nothing and printed no skip line, is the most common way this command fails.
259

261

267	
268	1. **`/command-name`**: Brief description of what to fix (specific context from critique findings)
269	2. **`/command-name`**: Brief description (specific context)
270	...
271	
272	**Rules for recommendations**:
273	- Only recommend commands from: /impeccable adapt, /impeccable animate, /impeccable audit, /impeccable bolder, /impeccable clarify, /impeccable colorize, /impeccable critique, /impeccable delight, /impeccable distill, /impeccable document, /impeccable harden, /impeccable layout, /impeccable onboard, /impeccable optimize, /impeccable overdrive, /impeccable polish, /impeccable quieter, /impeccable shape, /impeccable typeset
274	- Order by the user's stated priorities first, then by impact
275	- Each item's description should carry enough context that the command knows what to focus on
276	- Map each Priority Issue to the appropriate command

278	- If the user chose a limited scope, only include items within that scope
279	- If the user marked areas as off-limits, exclude commands that would touch those areas
280	- End with `/impeccable polish` as the final step if any fixes were recommended
281	
282	After presenting the summary, tell the user:
283	
284	> You can ask me to run these one at a time, all at once, or in any order you prefer.
285	>
286	> Re-run `/impeccable critique` after fixes to see your score improve.
